lessons.title: Threads
lessons.summary: Thread vs Runnable, start() vs run(), join, sleep and thread states.

blocks.text: A **thread** is an independent path of execution. Every program starts with one: the **main** thread. You can start more threads so work runs at the same time.
The work itself is a `Runnable`: a functional interface with one method, `void run()`. You hand it to a `Thread`, or you subclass `Thread` and override `run()`.

blocks.title: Prefer Runnable
blocks.text: Passing a `Runnable` keeps the task separate from the thread machinery, and your class can still extend something else. Executors (lesson 3) also take Runnables.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: It's like `threading.Thread(target=f)`, but there's no GIL: Java threads really run in parallel on several cores, so data races show up quickly.
`start()` creates a **new** thread, and that new thread calls `run()`. Calling `run()` yourself is just an ordinary method call: the code runs in the **current** thread.

blocks.title: The classic trap
blocks.text: Exam code often calls `run()` instead of `start()`. The output is then completely predictable, because nothing runs in parallel. Check every `run()` call: it never starts a thread.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `t.run()` is a plain method call, so the lambda runs in the **main** thread and `getName()` returns `main`. The name `worker` belongs to a thread that is never started.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `start()` runs `run()` once in the new thread and prints `R`. `join()` waits for it. Then `j.run()` is an ordinary call in main and prints `R` again. Calling `run()` on a finished thread is allowed; only a second `start()` is illegal.

blocks.text: `t.join()` makes the **current** thread wait until `t` has finished. That is how you make output predictable: wait first, then print.

blocks.caption: Always prints work, then done

items: `Thread.sleep(ms)` is **static**: it pauses the thread that calls it.
`join()` and `sleep()` both throw the checked `InterruptedException`.
`join(ms)` waits at most that long.

blocks.title: Checked exception
blocks.text: A method that calls `Thread.sleep()` or `join()` must catch `InterruptedException` or declare `throws InterruptedException`. Otherwise the code does not compile. Inside a `Runnable` lambda you must catch it, because `run()` declares no exceptions.

blocks.title: sleep keeps the lock, wait releases it
blocks.text: `Thread.sleep()` inside a `synchronized` block keeps the monitor the whole time, so other threads that want it stay `BLOCKED`. `obj.wait()` is different: it **releases** the monitor while waiting and takes it back before returning.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so a new thread prints A, and main prints B only after that thread has finished.
steps.explanation: `start()` launches the new thread; `join()` blocks main until it ends, so `A` is always printed before `B`. `wait()` without holding the monitor throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`, and `sleep()` is static and only pauses main.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that causes a compilation error.
steps.explanation: `Thread.sleep()` throws the checked `InterruptedException`. `rest()` neither catches it nor declares `throws InterruptedException`, so line 4 does not compile.

blocks.text: `t.getState()` returns a `Thread.State` enum value. A thread moves through these states:

blocks.title: One start per thread
blocks.text: A thread can be started only **once**. Calling `start()` again, even after it has terminated, throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

blocks.title: interrupt() only sets a flag
blocks.text: `t.interrupt()` doesn't stop `t`. It sets `t`'s **interrupt flag**. If `t` is in `sleep`, `join` or `wait` (or enters one), it wakes with `InterruptedException` and the flag is **cleared**. A `BLOCKED` thread waiting for a monitor is not woken: it keeps waiting.

blocks.caption: The exception clears the flag

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
No output; the second start() is ignored
steps.explanation: The first `start()` runs the empty task, and `join()` waits until it is `TERMINATED`. A thread can never be restarted: the second `start()` throws `IllegalThreadStateException`, so `again` is never printed.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: A thread inside Thread.sleep(500) is in TIMED_WAITING.
A thread waiting to enter a synchronized block is in WAITING.
A TERMINATED thread can be run again with start().
A thread calling t.join() with no timeout is in WAITING.
A newly constructed Thread is RUNNABLE.
steps.explanation: `sleep(500)` has a time limit, so the state is `TIMED_WAITING`; `join()` without a timeout is `WAITING`. A thread waiting for a monitor lock is `BLOCKED`, not `WAITING`. A new thread is `NEW` until `start()`, and a terminated thread can never be restarted.

blocks.text: A **daemon** thread is a background helper. The JVM exits as soon as only daemon threads are left; it does not wait for them.

items: `t.setDaemon(true)` must be called **before** `start()`, otherwise `IllegalThreadStateException`.
The main thread is not a daemon. New threads copy the daemon status of the thread that creates them.
Non-daemon (user) threads keep the JVM alive, even after `main` returns.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: If `main` ends while a daemon thread is still sleeping, that thread's later output may never appear. If it is a normal thread, the JVM waits for it.

steps.prompt: The JVM waits for all running daemon threads to finish before it exits.
steps.explanation: False. The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain; they are stopped abruptly. It waits only for non-daemon (user) threads.

lessons.title: Virtual threads
lessons.summary: Java 21's lightweight threads: how to create them and when to use them.

blocks.text: A classic **platform thread** wraps an operating-system thread. OS threads are expensive (a large stack, slow to create), so you can only have a few thousand.

A **virtual thread** (final in Java 21) is managed by the JVM. When it blocks, for example waiting on the network, the JVM unmounts it and reuses the underlying **carrier** platform thread for other work. You can have millions.

blocks.title: Not faster, just cheaper
blocks.text: Virtual threads don't make code run faster. They let you run many more tasks that spend most of their time waiting.
There is no public constructor for virtual threads: `new Thread(...)` always makes a **platform** thread. Use the builders or the static factory:

items: `start(task)` creates and starts; `unstarted(task)` only creates (state `NEW`).
`t.isVirtual()` tells you which kind you have.
Virtual threads are always daemon threads.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `new Thread` makes a platform thread, so `a.isVirtual()` is false. `ofVirtual().unstarted(...)` creates a virtual thread without starting it, so its state is `NEW`.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Virtual threads are **always** daemon threads. `setDaemon(false)` on a virtual thread throws `IllegalArgumentException`, so `ok` is never printed.

blocks.text: With virtual threads you don't keep a pool. You create a fresh thread for every task and let it die. The executor for that is:

blocks.title: Don't pool virtual threads
blocks.text: Pools exist because platform threads are expensive. Virtual threads are cheap, so pooling them buys nothing. To limit how many tasks hit a resource at once, use a `Semaphore`, not a smaller pool.

blocks.title: Imports
blocks.text: From here on, code samples assume `import java.util.concurrent.*;` (plus `.atomic.*` and `.locks.*` where needed). Exam questions say the same: assume the needed imports are present.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so each task runs in its own new virtual thread and prints true.
steps.explanation: `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` starts a new virtual thread per submitted task. `Thread.currentThread().isVirtual()` is then true. There is no `newVirtualExecutor()`, and `ofVirtual()` is a method of `Thread`, not `Executors`.

blocks.text: A virtual thread normally unmounts from its carrier when it blocks. In Java 21 there is an exception: if it blocks **inside a `synchronized` block or method**, it is **pinned**. The carrier thread is stuck too and can't run other virtual threads.

blocks.title: On the exam (Java 21)
blocks.text: Know the word **pinning** and the fix: for long blocking work inside a critical section, use a `ReentrantLock` (lesson 6) instead of `synchronized`. Short `synchronized` sections are fine.

steps.prompt: In Java 21, a virtual thread waits for a slow network call inside a synchronized block. What happens?
options: It is pinned: its carrier platform thread stays blocked too.
The JVM turns it into a platform thread.
steps.explanation: This is **pinning**: the virtual thread can't unmount while it holds a monitor, so its carrier platform thread is blocked as well. Nothing throws, and the thread does not change kind. Using `ReentrantLock` avoids it.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about virtual threads in Java 21 are true? Choose two.
options: new Thread(runnable) creates a virtual thread.
They should be pooled because they are expensive to create.
They suit many tasks that spend time blocked on I/O.
They make CPU-bound calculations run faster.
steps.explanation: Virtual threads are always daemon threads and shine when many tasks block on I/O. `new Thread(r)` always creates a platform thread. They are cheap, so you should **not** pool them. CPU-bound work gets no faster: the number of cores is the limit.

steps.prompt: `Thread.startVirtualThread(task)` creates a virtual thread and starts it in one call.
steps.explanation: True. It is a shortcut for `Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)` and returns the started `Thread`.

lessons.title: ExecutorService
lessons.summary: Thread pools, submit vs execute, Future, Callable, shutdown and scheduling.

steps.title: Let a pool run your tasks

blocks.text: Creating threads by hand gets messy. An `ExecutorService` owns a set of threads; you just **submit tasks** and it decides which thread runs them.

rows: grows as needed, reuses idle ones
n, can run tasks later or repeatedly
a new virtual thread per task

blocks.title: Single thread = ordered
blocks.text: A single-thread executor runs tasks one after another in submission order. That makes it handy for predictable output.

blocks.caption: A lambda that returns a value is a Callable

blocks.title: execute() is void
blocks.text: `execute()` returns nothing and only takes a `Runnable`. Code that assigns its result to a `Future` doesn't compile.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `execute()` returns `void` and accepts only a `Runnable`, so assigning its result to `Future<Integer>` fails at line 3. Use `submit()` to get a `Future`.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: Runnable.run() returns its result through Future.get().
Future.get() on a submitted Runnable returns null when it completes.
Callable is in the java.lang package.
steps.explanation: `Callable.call()` declares `throws Exception`, so it may throw checked exceptions. `submit(Runnable)` returns a `Future` whose `get()` returns `null` once the task completes. `execute()` takes only a `Runnable`, and `Callable` lives in `java.util.concurrent`, not `java.lang`.

blocks.text: A `Future` is a handle to a result that may not exist yet.

items: `get()` **blocks** until the task finishes, then returns its value.
`get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` gives up with `TimeoutException`.
`isDone()` is true once the task finished, failed or was cancelled.
`cancel(true)` tries to stop it (interrupting if running); `isCancelled()` reports it.
If the task threw, `get()` throws `ExecutionException` wrapping the cause.

blocks.text: **CompletableFuture** is beyond the core objectives, but worth knowing: a `Future` you can chain instead of blocking on.

items: `supplyAsync(supplier)` / `runAsync(runnable)` run on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` unless you pass an executor as a second argument.
`thenApply(fn)` transforms the result; `thenCompose(fn)` is for an `fn` that itself returns a `CompletableFuture` (like `flatMap`); `thenCombine(other, (a, b) -> ...)` merges two results.
`exceptionally(ex -> fallback)` recovers from a failure; `handle((value, ex) -> ...)` sees success and failure.

blocks.code:
int n = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 20)
    .thenApply(x -> x + 1)
    .thenCombine(
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 2),
        (a, b) -> a * b)
    .join();
int safe = CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> 1 / 0)
    .exceptionally(ex -> -1)
    .join();
System.out.println(n + " " + safe);

blocks.title: join vs get
blocks.text: `join()` wraps a failure in the **unchecked** `CompletionException`; `get()` throws the checked `ExecutionException` (and `InterruptedException`). A `thenApplyAsync(fn, exec)` stage is handed to `exec` only when the previous stage completes, so if `exec` was shut down by then you get a `RejectedExecutionException`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `f.get()` waits until the task has returned `"hi"`. Once `get()` has returned normally, the task is complete, so `isDone()` is `true`.

rows: no new tasks; queued and running tasks still finish
interrupts running tasks; returns `List<Runnable>` never started
blocks until all done or timeout; returns `boolean`
shutdown called / all tasks finished too

blocks.text: Since Java 19, `ExecutorService` is `AutoCloseable`, so try-with-resources shuts it down and waits:

blocks.title: Two classic traps
blocks.text: 1) Submitting after `shutdown()` throws `RejectedExecutionException`. 2) Forgetting to shut down a pool of normal threads keeps the JVM running after `main` ends.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: After `shutdown()` the executor rejects new tasks: `submit()` throws `RejectedExecutionException`. Neither `late` nor `end` is printed.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines: create a pool, submit a task, stop accepting tasks, wait for the pool to finish, then print the result.
steps.explanation: `shutdown()` must come after `submit()` (otherwise the task is rejected) and before `awaitTermination()` (otherwise it just waits for the timeout). `f.get()` then returns at once. Executors have no `start()` method.

items: `invokeAll(tasks)` runs a collection of `Callable`s, waits for **all**, and returns a `List<Future<T>>` in the same order.
`invokeAny(tasks)` waits for **one** to succeed, returns its value (not a Future) and cancels the rest.

steps.prompt: `invokeAny()` returns a List of Futures, one per task.
steps.explanation: False. That describes `invokeAll()`. `invokeAny()` returns a single plain result `T` from one task that completed successfully.

blocks.caption: SECONDS = TimeUnit.SECONDS (static import)

blocks.title: Runnable only for repeats
blocks.text: The two repeating methods take a `Runnable`, because a repeated task has no single result. Only `schedule()` also accepts a `Callable`.

steps.prompt: `ses` is a ScheduledExecutorService and `TimeUnit.SECONDS` is statically imported. Which two lines compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `schedule()` accepts a `Callable`, so `() -> "x"` is fine. `scheduleWithFixedDelay` with an empty Runnable and four arguments is fine. `scheduleAtFixedRate` needs a `Runnable` (`"x"` is not a statement) and four arguments; `schedule()` needs a delay before the unit.

steps.prompt: A task always takes 3 seconds. It is scheduled with `scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, 0, 2, SECONDS)`. How long is it from the start of one run to the start of the next?
steps.explanation: With a fixed **delay**, the 2-second wait starts when a run **ends**: 3 s of work + 2 s delay = 5 s between starts. With `scheduleAtFixedRate` and period 2, the next run would start as soon as the 3-second run finishes (runs never overlap).

lessons.title: Thread-safety problems
lessons.summary: Race conditions, lost updates, visibility, deadlock, livelock and starvation.

blocks.text: When two threads read and write the **same mutable data** without coordination, the result depends on timing. That's a **race condition**.
`count++` looks like one step but is three: **read** count, **add** 1, **write** it back. Two threads can both read 5, both write 6: one increment is lost.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: In CPython the GIL hides many races. Java threads run truly in parallel on several cores, so lost updates appear quickly and often.

steps.prompt: Which two outputs are possible? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `count[0]++` is not atomic, so the two threads can lose updates. `2000` happens when no update is lost; `1500` is a typical lost-update result. More than 2000 is impossible, and so is 0: every write stores a value of at least 1. The code compiles: `count` itself is effectively final, only the array element changes.

steps.prompt: `count++` on a shared `int` field is a single atomic operation.
steps.explanation: False. It is read, add, write: three steps that another thread can interleave with. Use `synchronized`, a lock or an `AtomicInteger`.

blocks.text: A second problem: without synchronization, a thread may **never see** another thread's write. Each core can keep values in its cache, and the compiler may reorder code.
The fix for a simple flag is `volatile` (next lesson). `synchronized`, locks, atomics and `join()` also guarantee that writes become visible.

steps.prompt: Which change guarantees that the code in the race-condition question always prints 2000?
options: Replace the array with an AtomicInteger and call incrementAndGet().
steps.explanation: An `AtomicInteger` with `incrementAndGet()` performs read-add-write as one atomic step. `volatile` on an array reference says nothing about its elements, and it wouldn't make `++` atomic anyway. `yield()` and start order only change timing.

rows: threads wait forever for locks held by each other; all stuck, `BLOCKED`
threads keep reacting to each other (back off, retry) and stay busy but make no progress
one thread rarely or never gets a resource because others keep taking it

blocks.caption: Opposite lock order: possible deadlock

blocks.title: Prevent deadlock
blocks.text: Make every thread acquire locks in the **same order** (always `a` then `b`), or use `tryLock` with a timeout and back off.

steps.prompt: Two threads each notice the other one wants the same resource, politely release it and retry. They repeat this forever: both are busy, neither finishes. What is this called?
steps.explanation: Threads that stay **active** but make no progress because they keep responding to each other are in a **livelock**. In a deadlock they would be stuck, not busy.

steps.prompt: A low-priority thread almost never gets a lock because other threads keep grabbing it first. Nothing is stuck and the others make progress. What is this called?
steps.explanation: One thread being unable to get a resource for a long time while others proceed is **starvation**. Fair locks (`new ReentrantLock(true)`) reduce it.

steps.prompt: If every thread acquires locks in the same order, two threads can't deadlock over those locks.
steps.explanation: True. A deadlock needs a cycle: thread 1 holds A and wants B while thread 2 holds B and wants A. A fixed global lock order makes that cycle impossible.

lessons.title: synchronized, volatile, atomics
lessons.summary: Monitors, which lock a method uses, volatile visibility and AtomicInteger.

blocks.text: Every object has a built-in lock called its **monitor**. Only one thread at a time can hold it. `synchronized` takes the monitor on entry and releases it on exit, even when an exception is thrown.

blocks.title: Same lock or not?
blocks.text: Exclusion only happens between threads using the **same** monitor. A `static synchronized` method and an instance `synchronized` method use different locks, so they can run at the same time.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `inc()` is `synchronized` on the same `Counter`, so no increment is lost. `join()` waits for both threads and makes their writes visible to main: the result is always **2000**.

steps.prompt: In class Shop, which two use the same lock as `synchronized void m()`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: An instance `synchronized` method locks `this`. A `synchronized (this)` block and any other instance `synchronized` method of the same object use that monitor too. `static synchronized` and `synchronized (Shop.class)` lock the Class object; a `new Object()` is a fresh lock every time.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that causes a compilation error.
steps.explanation: `synchronized` needs an object reference to use as the monitor. `count` is a primitive `int`, so line 6 doesn't compile. (It is not autoboxed.)

blocks.text: A `volatile` field is always read from and written to main memory, so every thread sees the **latest** value. It also stops the compiler from reordering code around it.

blocks.title: Visibility, not atomicity
blocks.text: `volatile int count; count++;` is **still** a race: two threads can read the same value. `volatile` is right for flags that one thread writes; use atomics or locks for read-modify-write. `volatile` is only allowed on fields, not local variables.

steps.prompt: Declaring a field `volatile int count` makes `count++` safe to call from many threads at once.
steps.explanation: False. `volatile` guarantees each read sees the latest write, but `count++` is still read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value and one update is lost.

blocks.text: `java.util.concurrent.atomic` has `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `AtomicBoolean` and `AtomicReference`. Their methods are atomic without any lock.

rows: `true` if it was `e` and is now `n`

blocks.title: Read the name left to right
blocks.text: **get**AndIncrement: get first, then increment (old value). increment**AndGet**: increment first, then get (new value).
Sometimes you avoid sharing altogether. A `ThreadLocal` gives **each thread its own copy** of a value. `ThreadLocal.withInitial(supplier)` sets the starting value per thread.

blocks.caption: Each thread sees its own value

blocks.title: remove() on pooled threads
blocks.text: Pool threads are reused. A value set by one task is still there for the next task on that thread. Call `remove()` in a `finally` when the task is done.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `getAndIncrement()` returns 10, value 11. `incrementAndGet()` makes it 12 and returns 12. `getAndAdd(5)` returns the old 12, value 17.

steps.prompt: Complete the thread-safe counter. hit() must return the count including this hit.
steps.explanation: `AtomicInteger` gives atomic updates. `incrementAndGet()` returns the **new** value; `getAndIncrement()` would return the old one (0 on the first hit). There is no `VolatileInteger` class, and `Integer` is immutable with no such methods.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: volatile guarantees other threads see the latest written value.
A static synchronized method locks on this.
volatile can be applied to local variables.
A constructor can be declared synchronized.
steps.explanation: `volatile` gives visibility of the latest write, and `incrementAndGet()` is atomic. A `static synchronized` method locks the Class object, not `this` (there is no `this` in a static method). `volatile` is not allowed on local variables, and constructors can't be `synchronized`: both fail to compile.

lessons.title: The Lock API
lessons.summary: ReentrantLock, tryLock, reentrancy, read/write locks and fairness.

blocks.text: `java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock` is an explicit lock. `ReentrantLock` is the standard implementation. You lock and unlock it yourself, so **always unlock in `finally`**.

blocks.title: Not released automatically
blocks.text: Nothing unlocks a `Lock` for you. If `unlock()` is not in `finally`, an exception leaves it locked forever, and other threads block forever.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines to update `balance` safely. Take the lock before entering the try block.
steps.explanation: The idiom is `lock()`, then `try`, then release in `finally`. If `lock()` were inside `try` and threw, `finally` would call `unlock()` on a lock it never acquired. `Lock` has no `release()` method.

items: `tryLock()` returns `true` and takes the lock if it is free, otherwise returns `false` **immediately**.
`tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)` waits up to the timeout; it throws `InterruptedException`.
Only call `unlock()` if you actually got the lock.

blocks.title: Unlocking a lock you don't hold
blocks.text: `unlock()` by a thread that does not hold the lock throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `A` is printed, then `finally` calls `unlock()` on a lock that was never acquired. That throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`, so `B` is never printed.

steps.prompt: Complete the code: take the lock only if it is free right now, and always release it.
steps.explanation: `tryLock()` returns a boolean, so it fits in `if`. `lock()` returns `void` and wouldn't compile there. The release belongs in `finally` so it also runs if the body throws. `Lock` has no `release()` method.

blocks.text: **Reentrant** means the thread that holds the lock can lock it again without blocking itself. The lock counts how often: the **hold count**. It is free only after the same number of `unlock()` calls.

blocks.title: synchronized is reentrant too
blocks.text: A `synchronized` method can call another `synchronized` method on the same object without deadlocking itself.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `lock()` makes the hold count 1. `tryLock()` by the **same** thread succeeds because the lock is reentrant: count 2. One `unlock()` leaves 1.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Main holds the lock while `t` runs. `t` is a different thread, so `tryLock()` can't take it and returns `false` immediately; it doesn't wait. `join()` makes sure `t` has printed before main unlocks.

blocks.text: `ReentrantReadWriteLock` has two linked locks. Many threads may hold the **read** lock together; the **write** lock is exclusive (no readers, no other writer).
`new ReentrantLock(true)` creates a **fair** lock: the longest-waiting thread gets it next. That prevents starvation but is slower. The default (`false`) lets threads barge in.

You can **downgrade**: take the read lock while holding the write lock, then release the write lock. You can't **upgrade**: the write lock is unavailable while any read lock is held, even your own, so `tryLock()` returns `false` and `lock()` waits forever.

blocks.title: StampedLock (beyond the core)
blocks.text: `StampedLock` adds an **optimistic read**: `long s = sl.tryOptimisticRead();` read the fields, then `if (!sl.validate(s))` a writer got in, so fall back to `sl.readLock()`. It is **not reentrant**.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Expect questions on: unlock in `finally`, `tryLock()` returning immediately, `IllegalMonitorStateException`, hold counts, and "many readers or one writer".

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: Several threads can hold a ReentrantReadWriteLock's read lock at once.
new ReentrantLock(true) creates a fair lock.
A ReentrantLock is released automatically when the try block ends.
tryLock() with no arguments waits until the lock is free.
Calling unlock() more times than lock() is silently ignored.
steps.explanation: Read locks are shared among readers, and the `true` constructor argument makes a lock fair. A `Lock` is never released automatically, `tryLock()` without arguments returns at once, and extra `unlock()` calls throw `IllegalMonitorStateException`.

lessons.title: Concurrent collections
lessons.summary: ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, BlockingQueue, latches and barriers.

blocks.text: `ArrayList`, `HashMap` and friends are **not** thread-safe. Two threads adding at once can corrupt them. Even a single thread that changes a list while iterating it gets a `ConcurrentModificationException` (CME).

blocks.title: Wrappers
blocks.text: `Collections.synchronizedList(list)` (and `synchronizedMap`, ...) locks every single method call. But iterating is several calls, so you must still wrap the loop in `synchronized (list) { }` yourself.

items: Thread-safe without locking the whole map; reads don't block.
`merge`, `compute`, `computeIfAbsent`, `putIfAbsent` are **atomic**.
Iterators never throw CME; they may or may not show concurrent changes.
**No null** keys or values: `put(null, ...)` throws `NullPointerException`.

blocks.title: HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap
blocks.text: `HashMap` allows one `null` key and `null` values. `ConcurrentHashMap` (and `Hashtable`) allow neither.
The 3-argument constructor `new ConcurrentHashMap<>(initialCapacity, loadFactor, concurrencyLevel)` only gives sizing hints; the map behaves the same.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `ConcurrentHashMap` rejects `null` keys and values. `put(null, 2)` throws `NullPointerException`. With a `HashMap` the output would be `2`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `merge()` on a `ConcurrentHashMap` is atomic, so no update is lost. After both `join()` calls, the value is exactly 2 x 500 = **1000**.

blocks.text: Every write (`add`, `remove`, `set`) copies the whole internal array. An iterator keeps working on the **snapshot** from when it was created: it never throws CME and never sees later changes.

blocks.caption: The loop only sees 1 and 2

blocks.title: When to use it
blocks.text: Good when reads vastly outnumber writes (lists of listeners, configuration). Bad for frequent writes: each one copies the array.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The for-each loop iterates over a snapshot of `[a, b, c]`, so it visits all three and prints `abc` even though each is removed from the live list. No CME. Afterwards the list is empty: `0`.

steps.prompt: With `Collections.synchronizedList(...)`, iterating in a for-each loop is safe while other threads add elements, without any extra locking.
steps.explanation: False. Each single method is synchronized, but iteration is many calls. You must hold the list's lock yourself: `synchronized (list) { for (...) ... }`. Otherwise a CME is possible.

blocks.text: A `BlockingQueue` connects **producer** threads with **consumer** threads. Its methods come in four flavours:

blocks.title: Bounded or not
blocks.text: `ArrayBlockingQueue(n)` always has a capacity. `LinkedBlockingQueue` is unbounded unless you pass a capacity. `put()` and `take()` throw `InterruptedException`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Capacity is 1. `offer("a")` succeeds: `true`. The queue is full, so `offer("b")` returns `false` instead of blocking. `poll()` returns `a`, then the empty queue gives `null`.

rows: N threads wait for each other

blocks.text: A **`Semaphore`** holds a number of permits. `acquire()` takes one (waiting if none is left), `tryAcquire()` returns `false` instead of waiting, and `release()` gives one back. Use it to cap how many threads use a resource at once.

items: Release in a `finally`, just like a lock.
Permits aren't owned: any thread may `release()`, even one that never acquired.
`new Semaphore(n, true)` is fair: waiting threads get permits in order.

blocks.title: Phaser
blocks.text: A `Phaser` is a reusable barrier where the party count can change. `register()` adds a party, `arriveAndAwaitAdvance()` waits for all parties, `arriveAndDeregister()` arrives and leaves. Each time everyone arrives, `getPhase()` goes up by one, starting at 0.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Both threads must reach `await()`. The last one to arrive runs the barrier action, printing `go`, before either thread continues. Main joins both, then prints `end`.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: A CountDownLatch can be reset and reused after reaching zero.
A CyclicBarrier can be reused after all parties have arrived.
BlockingQueue.take() waits until an element is available.
Iterating a ConcurrentHashMap while another thread changes it throws ConcurrentModificationException.
steps.explanation: A `CyclicBarrier` resets after each trip and can be reused; `take()` blocks until an element arrives. A `CountDownLatch` can't be reset. `ConcurrentHashMap` forbids null values, and its iterators never throw CME.

lessons.title: Parallel streams
lessons.summary: Splitting stream work across threads, ordering, and the side-effect trap.

blocks.text: Call `.parallel()` on a stream, or `parallelStream()` on a collection. The work is split into chunks that run on threads of the shared **ForkJoinPool.commonPool()**, and the partial results are combined.

items: `isParallel()` tells you whether a stream is parallel; `.sequential()` switches back.
Built-in reductions (`sum`, `count`, `collect`, `toList`) give the same result as sequential.
What changes is **order of side effects** such as printing.

blocks.text: Under the hood is the **Fork/Join** framework. You extend `RecursiveTask<V>` (returns a value) or `RecursiveAction` (returns nothing) and override `compute()`: if the job is small, do it; otherwise split it, `fork()` one half, compute the other, then `join()`.

blocks.caption: Prints 4950

blocks.title: Work stealing
blocks.text: Each `ForkJoinPool` worker has its own queue of tasks. An idle worker **steals** tasks from a busy one's queue, so splitting work keeps all cores busy. Parallel streams use the same common pool.

steps.prompt: Which two outputs are possible? Choose two.
steps.code:
List.of(1, 2, 3).parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::print);
steps.explanation: `forEach` on a parallel stream runs the action on several threads in no particular order, so any arrangement of 1, 2, 3 is possible, including `123` and `321`. Each element is printed exactly once, so `12` and `1233` are impossible. The code compiles.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `Stream.of` is ordered, and `collect(Collectors.toList())` keeps encounter order even in parallel. Parallelism changes **which thread** maps each element, not where the result lands.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `findFirst()` respects encounter order, even on a parallel stream: always `5`. Only `findAny()` may return any element.

blocks.text: Adding to a plain `ArrayList` from a parallel `forEach` is a race. Elements can go missing, `null`s can appear, or an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` is thrown.

blocks.title: Let the stream collect
blocks.text: Prefer `collect(...)` / `toList()` over adding to an outside collection. If you must use side effects, the target has to be thread-safe, and even then its order is unpredictable.

blocks.title: Identity must be neutral
blocks.text: `reduce(identity, op)` in parallel may apply the identity once **per chunk**. `reduce(0, Integer::sum)` is fine; `reduce(1, Integer::sum)` can give different results on different runs.

steps.prompt: A parallel stream calls `forEach(list::add)` for 1000 elements. Which two kinds of `list` always end up with size 1000? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `CopyOnWriteArrayList` and a `Collections.synchronizedList` wrapper make each `add` thread-safe, so no element is lost (the order still varies). `ArrayList` and `LinkedList` are not thread-safe, and `List.of()` is immutable: `add` throws.

steps.prompt: What is true about this code's output?
options: It can be more than 11, because the identity may be used once per chunk.
steps.explanation: The identity `1` is not neutral for addition. A parallel stream may start several chunks from the identity, adding 1 per chunk, so results larger than 11 (up to 14) are possible and can vary between runs. Sequentially it would always be 11.

steps.prompt: Adding `.parallel()` to a stream always makes it run faster.
steps.explanation: False. Splitting and combining costs time. For small data or cheap operations, a parallel stream is often slower. It pays off for large, CPU-heavy, independent work.

lessons.title: Unit 8 checkpoint
lessons.summary: 12 exam-style questions on threads, executors, locking and concurrent collections.

blocks.text: 12 exam-style questions covering the whole unit. Assume all needed `java.util.concurrent` imports are present.

blocks.title: Exam habit
blocks.text: For concurrency code, first ask: is anything really running in parallel (`start()` or just `run()`)? Is there a `join()`/`get()` before the print? Is the shared update atomic? Only then pick an output.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `start()` runs the lambda in the new thread named `T1`, and `join()` waits for it: `T1`. Then `t.run()` is a plain method call in main: `main`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: The lambda `() -> System.out.print(...)` is void, so it is submitted as a `Runnable`. `get()` waits for it to finish and then returns `null`.

steps.prompt: `ex` is an ExecutorService. Which two lines compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `submit()` accepts a value-returning lambda as a `Callable<Integer>`. `execute()` with a void lambda is a valid `Runnable`. `execute()` returns `void`; a `Callable` must return a value; `() -> 1` is not a valid `Runnable` body.

steps.prompt: What does `shutdownNow()` return?
options: A List<Runnable> of tasks that never started
A boolean: whether all tasks finished
A List<Future<?>> of all submitted tasks
steps.explanation: `shutdownNow()` interrupts running tasks and returns the tasks that were still waiting in the queue, as a `List<Runnable>`. `awaitTermination()` is the one returning a boolean.

steps.prompt: Which two outputs are possible? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Virtual threads are daemon threads. `main` returns without `join()`, so the JVM may exit before or after the virtual thread prints. Both `hi` and no output are possible. The code compiles, and `hi` can be printed at most once.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `incrementAndGet()` is atomic, so the parallel `forEach` loses no increments. `forEach` is a terminal operation that returns only when all elements are processed: always `100`.

steps.prompt: What is printed?
steps.explanation: `volatile` makes the latest value visible, but `count++` is still read, add, write. Updates can be lost, so the result may be anything up to 2000, not just 2000.

steps.prompt: Thread 1 is inside `Box.a()`. Thread 2 calls `b()` on a Box object. What happens?
options: Thread 2 runs b() at once; the two locks are different.
steps.explanation: `static synchronized` locks `Box.class`; instance `synchronized` locks the Box object. Different monitors, so the methods don't exclude each other and thread 2 runs `b()` right away.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Main holds a read lock. Read locks are shared, so `t` gets one too: `true`. The write lock needs no readers at all, and two are active, so `tryLock()` returns `false` at once.

steps.prompt: A task takes 1 second. It is scheduled with `scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 3, SECONDS)`. When does its third run start?
steps.explanation: At a fixed **rate**, runs start every 3 s from the first start: 0 s, 3 s, 6 s. With `scheduleWithFixedDelay` the gap would be 1 s of work + 3 s, giving 0, 4 and 8 s.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: Collections.synchronizedMap() lets reads skip the lock.
LinkedBlockingQueue.offer(e) blocks when the queue is full.
A CyclicBarrier can be used only once.
steps.explanation: `CopyOnWriteArrayList` iterates a snapshot and never throws CME. `ConcurrentHashMap` rejects null keys with `NullPointerException`. A synchronized wrapper locks every call, including reads. `offer()` returns `false` instead of blocking, and a `CyclicBarrier` is reusable.

steps.prompt: `ex.shutdown()` was called and then `ex.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` returns `false`. What does that mean?
options: The timeout elapsed before all tasks finished.
Every task finished with an exception.
The executor was cancelled and its tasks discarded.
shutdown() failed and the executor accepts tasks again.
steps.explanation: `awaitTermination()` returns `true` if the executor terminated within the timeout and `false` if the time ran out first. Tasks are still running; nothing was cancelled.
